Table 6: Application of the accuracy-sparsity metrics (Sec. 4.3) to compare PDEA versus PDEB using validation data V simulated from the KS ground truth PDEGT as reference. Note that N/A means “Not Applicable” because Score is conditional on the increase in complexity (in our case from PDEA to PDEB) and not the other way around.

Figure 2: Simulated solutions of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation PDEGT (left) and 2 learned equations, PDEA (center) and PDEB (right). For the purpose of this running example, PDEA is by construction much more similar to the ground truth than PDEB. Indeed, we can observe that PDEB gradually diverges over time from the true physical dynamics modeled by PDEGT .

Figure 7: Long-horizon simulations (T ∈ [0, 300]) of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsk GT PDEGT (left), PDEA (center) and PDEB (right). The rollout error ϵtrollout(û, u) over time (dashed-lines) is also reported.

Figure 1: Overview of PDE discovery and metrics (in blue) devoted to address the multifaceted challenge of post-hoc PDE evaluation in accordance with the five key principles to be met (in red). The illustrations of dynamics correspond to a physical system leading to complex pattern formation and chaotic behavior. They are simulated from either the ground truth Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (PDEGT ) or a learned PDEA, or they correspond to observation data (e.g. obtained by laser-matter interaction and self-organization of matter for which PDEGT is a good candidate for modeling the phenomenon). Three sets are used in PDE discovery: a training set T is employed for learning PDEA with some algorithm A; a validation set V is compared to a set E of estimated solutions, simulated from PDEA, for evaluating the discovered law from a pointwise or trajectory perspective.

Figure 4: Possible pitfall of over-interpreting small residuals: 3D solutions of the KuramotoSivashinsky equation PDEGT (left) and solutions simulated from a learned equation that would satisfy the initial/boundary conditions and return 0 everywhere else (right), leading thus to zero residuals.

Table 7: Capacity of out-of-distribution generalization of PDEA and PDEB in three scenarios: (i) varying initial conditions IC. The MAE is used as evaluation metric. Note that IC1 corresponds to the conditions of the running example; (ii) longer horizons at different times T ≥ 50. The rollout error is evaluated at time 50, 100, 200 and 300; (iii) mesh and time convergence.

Table 2: Application of the term recovery metrics (Sec. 3.1) to compare PDEA versus PDEB using the KS ground truth PDEGT as reference. A green point • (resp. •) corresponds to a better (resp. worse) evaluation score w.r.t. PDEGT . By construction of the equations, PDEA is expected to achieve better scores. An • point corresponds to a tie situation, where the metric is unable to distinguish between the two PDEs.

Table 1: Capacity of the investigated metrics to answer the 5 key questions in PDE evaluation. The last four rows of the table do not, strictly speaking, represent evaluation metrics, but rather physical properties discussed in Sec. 4.4 that can be used to assess the physical consistency of the PDE.
